species_affected.value: hedgehogs, feeder mice/rats, turtles, fish (other sources in the same year)

pathogen.value: Salmonella (several serotypes, including Montevideo, Hadar, Infantis, Newport and Lille found on live poultry)

how_it_spreads.value: handling live poultry such as chicks and ducklings from hatcheries, then touching the mouth or food without washing hands
poultry can carry Salmonella in their gut without looking sick, spreading it through their droppings to soil, other animals, and manure-fertilized crops
birds crowded together in hatcheries increases spread among poultry

key_symptoms.value: fever, abdominal pain, nausea and diarrhea in infected people, lasting up to about a week

mortality.value: three separate 2012 live-poultry outbreaks caused a combined 3 deaths among roughly 330 human cases in the US

incubation_period.value: symptoms in people usually appear 12 to 72 hours after exposure

prevention.value: wash hands after handling live poultry, reptiles or other animals and after using the restroom
avoid cross-contaminating other foods with raw poultry
cook food thoroughly (to at least 167°F/75°C for 10 minutes)

summary.value: In 2012 several unrelated Salmonella outbreaks occurred worldwide from sources including live baby chicks and ducklings sold by hatcheries, alongside outbreaks from turtles, hedgehogs, feeder rodents, tuna and smoked salmon. It illustrates that backyard-keepers can catch salmonellosis from healthy-looking chicks or hens, so hand-washing after handling birds is important.
